# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1-37 (Extended v238)

## Setting and Time
Multiple periods spanning French Revolution to summer Year 10, and 1784-1820 (Marseilles/Pharaon timeline). Key Paris locations: Rue Plumet, Place de la Bastille, Prison Chargemagne, Rue de l'Homme Armé No. 6, Champ-de-Mars, Halles district, Rue de la Chanvrerie, Champs-Élysées, Rue Saint-Honoré, Luxembourg Garden, Quai aux Fleurs, Rue du Temple, sewers (Sainte-Avoye, Louvre, Montmartre, belt, Amelot, Beautreillis), Marais, Blancs-Manteaux, Rue Culture-Sainte-Catherine, Rue de l'Écharpe, Rue Pavée, Rue des Trois-Pavillons, Saint-Paul church, Rue Beautreillis near Arsenal, Grand Sewer, Rue de l'Hôpital, Père-Lachaise cemetery, Rue Mondétour, Tuileries, Rue Saint-Jacques, Rue de la Jussienne, Rue Coq-Héron, Rue Bussy, Lyons, Grenoble. English locations: Kelmere, Elmhaven, Ostcombe, Dungate, Ravenmere, Staveford, Wilwick, Salcombe, Wilholt, Torton, Yarlby, Gagny, Lagny, Gulhaven. Marseilles: La Canebière, Rue de Noailles, Allées de Meilhan, Rue du Grand Cours, Rue de l'Homme Armé, Medusa fountain, Palais de Justice, Accoules clock-tower, Rue Caisserie, Rue Saint-Laurent, Rue Taramis, La Consigne, Frioul, Pilon, Porto-Ferrajo, Naples, Elba, Island of Elba, Point des Catalans, Ile Ratonneau, Rue de la Loge, Catalans, Madrid, Cape Pharo, Cape de Morgiou, Château d'If. **Timeline: 1814-1820 Marseilles; 1 March 1814 Dantès' arrest; spring Year 10 (1833) current time in English subplot; 30 July 1816 Dantès' prison reckoning.**

## English Subplot Summary (through Chapter 37, spring Year 10)

**Established solemn promises**: Semor swore to Isric Thornmere to rebuild fallen wall at Kelmere (summer Year 9). Elra gave Matho promise to plant orchard on slope above Gulhaven; Pelia gave Fenelle promise to plant orchard above Salcombe (summer Year 7); Movie swore to Nerine promise to plant orchard above Wilholt (autumn Year 7); Yera Haskick swore to Nerine Prydenridge to repair chapel roof at Kelmere (winter Year 8); Kassa Stenson kept promise to Taric Corrley: wall at Yarlby rebuilt by harvest; Kassa's husband swore to rebuild fallen wall at Ostcombe. Yera Haskick gave Lurald Stenworth solemn promise to carry sealed letter to Quenford (winter Year 9). Eldest daughter of Lura Haskick kept promise made to Nerine Prydenridge: chapel roof repair at Kelmere completed by harvest (winter Year 9). Fewyn gave Havus Stenworth solemn promise to carry a sealed letter to Salcombe (winter Year 9). Luena gave husband of Yera Stenworth solemn promise to pay old debt owed to Haskick family (winter Year 9). **Sebin swore to youngest daughter of Havus Stenworth to repair roof of chapel at Wilholt** (spring Year 10).

**Chapter 34-35 migrations**: Taric Corrley moved from Dungate to Kelmere with Kassa Stenson. Luena Stenenridge's only son moved from Ostcombe to Elmhaven. Pelde Stenworth married Sebin Brackick at Torton; couple lived in Torton thereafter. Fewyn Stenworth moved from Gulhaven to Yarlby with Havus. Pelia Lindmere moved to Yarlby with Rorald Lindmere. Havie Prydenridge found work in Staveford, moved there; Isric Thornmere followed her within the month. Youngest daughter of Fewyn Stenworth was apprenticed anew and became a herbalist. Youngest son of Nelan Brackick was apprenticed anew and became a weaver.

**Chapter 36-37 winter/spring scenes and rumors**: Frost silvered hedges; light went early; gulls quarreled over fish heads by steps; smoke lay flat over fields; wind carried salt and tar smell; road rutted and puddled after thaw. Bees hummed in lavender behind parsonage. Children chased hoop down lane; rain threatened since morning but held off; dog barked at nothing then went quiet; baker's boy late, line at oven grew long. Multiple characters hummed childhood tunes while scrubbing steps (Rovus, Ismira, Isric, Yewyn, Movus). Ismira and Movus fell asleep in chairs before fire caught. Ismira laughed at story nobody else found funny. **RUMOR—Isric Thornmere told Havie Prydenridge old abbey at Gulhaven hides second cellar.** Movus Brackick bought ribbon at stall and regretted it; counted coins twice, came up penny short. Isric Thornmere won copper chalice from Gadrek Prydenridge at cards fairly. Jotho Thornmere mended torn sleeve. **Late one night Kassa Brackick confided to Davus that Stenenridge mill ledger was rewritten after flood.** Someone chalked crooked sun on forge wall. Cart loaded with turnips creaked past well. Movus mended torn sleeve by window, said little. Rorald and Fewyn Stenworth talked of weather, harvest, lame horse. Rorald read almanac aloud, mispronouncing saints. Yewyn Haskick complained of aching back. Salt price repeatedly discussed; Gadrek laughed at story nobody else found funny; Rozek Stenenridge pressed jade mirror into Luvie Prydenridge's hands; Yewyn and Rozek sorted old letters by candlelight; Rorald Lindmere and others sorted letters; Havus fell asleep in chair; Luvie remarked river was up again. **Ismira Stenson died that summer from festering wound; buried at Kelmere.** **A son born to Luvie Prydenridge and Semor Brackick, named Brevus Brackick; family lived in Ostcombe.** Yewyn Corrford complained of aching back as usual; mentioned salt price scandal. Yewyn Corrford hummed childhood tune while scrubbing step. Rovus Prydenridge told Wenelle he looked tired; Wenelle did not deny it. Brevus read almanac aloud, mispronouncing half the saints. Brevus spent evening sorting old letters by candlelight. Wenelle Lindmere bought ribbon at stall and regretted it. **Multiple characters asked: "Will it rain, do you think?"** (Gadrek to Nerine; Luena to Lurald; Luena to Brevus Brackick; Rovus to Wenelle). **The bone compass which Ismira Stenson had owned went to Matho Stenson.** **Kadan counted the coins twice and still came up a penny short.** **Yewyn walked the long way round to avoid the muddy square.** **Febin Prydenridge and Yewyn Corrford talked of nothing much—the weather, the harvest, a lame horse.** **Davus remarked salt price is a scandal; Elvie Brackick agreed.** **Pelde Stenworth gave birth to daughter, named Elvie Brackick; father was Sebin Brackick; family lived in Torton.** **Ilrald Prydenridge and Pelde talked of nothing much—weather, harvest, lame horse.** **Pelde Stenworth laughed at story nobody else found funny.** **Pelde Stenson fell asleep in chair before fire had caught.** Harine and Davus discussed river being up in spring. **Kadrek Brackick argued with the carter over the price of a sack of oats.** **Rinelle counted the coins twice and still came up a penny short.** **Ilrald counted the coins twice and still came up a penny short.** **Luvie Prydenridge meant to go to Kelmere before the frost, but the roads flooded and the journey was put off.** **Luena Stenenridge walked the long way round to avoid the muddy square.** **Brevus told Yera he looked tired; Yera did not deny it.** **Gadrek Prydenridge mended a torn sleeve by the window and said little.** **Rozek Stenenridge bought a ribbon at the stall and then regretted it.** **Nerine spent the evening sorting old letters by candlelight.** **Rozek Stenenridge and Luena talked of nothing much—the weather, the harvest, a lame horse.** **Matho laughed at a story nobody else found funny.**

## Marseilles/Pharaon Subplot (1814-1820): Dantès' Arrest to Starvation Attempt

**Edmond Dantès' arrival and engagement (1814)**: Young sailor Edmond Dantès jumped into skiff at La Canebière. Dantès ascended Allées de Meilhan, found father training nasturtiums and clematis. Reported Captain Leclere dead; would become captain with M. Morrel's aid. Captain at twenty, hundred louis pay, share in profits. Observed greedy glance in Caderousse's dark eyes.

**Fernand and Mercédès tragedy**: Fernand begged Mercédès to repeat refusal; ten years of marriage dreams ruined. Mercédès replied she never encouraged hope; always said she loved him as brother; heart belonged to another. **When Fernand asked final determination, Mercédès declared: if misfortune occur to Edmond, she would ascend Cape de Morgiou and cast herself headlong from it.** Later, Dantès and Mercédès clasped in each other's arms. Dantès saw Fernand's gloomy, pale, threatening countenance; Fernand placed hand on knife; Dantès extended cordial hand; Fernand remained mute and trembling.

**Danglars' denunciation and Caderousse's intervention**: Danglars feared being between drunkard and coward. Proposed to Fernand: write denunciation with left hand (handwriting unrecognizable). Wrote letter to king's attorney naming Edmond Dantès as Murat's agent carrying letters for usurper and Bonapartist committee. Caderousse, after reading letter, comprehended misery it must entail: "Yes, and that's all settled; only it will be an infamous shame." Stretched hand to reach letter; Danglars took it beyond reach, claimed jest, squeezed letter and threw into arbor corner. Earlier, Caderousse said: "Kill Dantès! who talks of killing Dantès? I won't have him killed. He's my friend, and this morning offered to share his money with me."

**1814 wedding and feast at La Réserve (1 March morning)**: M. Morrel had repeated promise that Dantès should succeed late Captain Leclere. Edmond placed arm of affianced bride within that of M. Morrel. Mercédès, lovely as Greek girls, with bright flashing jet eyes and ripe coral lips, moved with light, free step. At table centre, Mercédès said "Father," pointing to father on her right; on her left she placed Fernand, "him who has ever been as a brother to me," with soft, gentle smile. Her words inflicted direst torture on Fernand; his lips became ghastly pale. Dantès' old father carried glass of topaz-hued wine to lips. Dantès explained: "Thanks to M. Morrel's influence, all difficulties removed. Permission waived usual delay; at half-past two o'clock Mayor of Marseilles will be waiting at city hall. Tomorrow he starts for Paris; four days to go, four to return, one to discharge commission, back by first of March. On second he gives real marriage feast."

**Arrest and Villefort's interrogation (1 March, during feast)**: Danglars, observing Fernand's look, saw him stagger and fall convulsively against seat near open window. Indistinct sound on stairs, measured tread of soldiery, clanking of swords. Loud voice: "I demand admittance in the name of the law!" Magistrate wearing official scarf presented himself with four soldiers and corporal. Announced: "I am bearer of order of arrest." M. Morrel felt resistance useless. Old Dantès prayed and supplicated; Dantès surrendered. Long terrified silence followed. Old father and Mercédès remained apart absorbed in grief; at length rushed into each other's arms. Fernand appeared, poured glass of water with trembling hand, sat next to Mercédès, instinctively drew back chair. Villefort took packet from gendarme, disappeared. Dantès entered pale but calm, saluting judge with easy politeness. When asked political opinions, Dantès replied: "I never had any opinions. I am hardly nineteen... I love my father, I respect M. Morrel, and I adore Mercédès." **Regarding Captain Leclere's death and commission: "What I ought to have done, and what everyone would have done in my place... I sailed for Island of Elba, arrived next day; found difficulty obtaining access to grand-marshal; sent ring received from captain; was instantly admitted. He questioned me concerning Captain Leclere's death; gave me letter to carry to person in Paris. I undertook it because it was what my captain bade me do."** Villefort said: "This seems truth... Give up letter from Elba, pass word you will appear if required, go rejoin friends." **Villefort had destroyed the fatal letter—only proof against Dantès.**

**Villefort's remorse and decision to sacrifice Dantès (1 March evening)**: First pangs of unending torture seized Villefort's heart. Innocent victim Edmond appeared pale and threatening, leading Mercédès by hand, bringing remorse—slow and consuming agony. **Mercédès, hearing no news, came unobserved to inquire after him at Villefort's door.** Villefort pushed by her, closed door. But remorse not thus banished; like Virgil's wounded hero, he carried arrow in his wound. At salon, uttered sigh almost a sob, sank into chair. If sweet voice of Renée had pleaded for mercy, or fair Mercédès entered with plea, his cold trembling hands would have signed release; but no voice broke stillness. Door opened only by valet announcing travelling carriage. Villefort sprang from chair, hastily opened drawer, emptied gold into pocket, stood motionless hand pressed to head, muttered inarticulate sounds. **The hapless Dantès was doomed.**

**Villefort stands watching Noirtier's escape and travel to Lyons/Marseilles**: Villefort stood breathing, watching until father Noirtier disappeared at Rue Bussy. Then Villefort put black cravat and blue frock-coat at bottom of portmanteau, threw hat into dark closet, broke cane into small bits and flung in fire, put on travelling-cap, called valet, paid bill, sprang into carriage which was ready, learned at Lyons that Bonaparte had entered Grenoble, and reached Marseilles prey to hopes and fears of ambition and its first successes.

**Villefort's audience with King Louis XVIII and Noirtier's transformation**: Villefort arrived at Tuileries in dusty garb. King Louis XVIII sat before walnut table from Hartwell, carelessly listening to Blacas' warnings of Napoleon's danger. Villefort reported discovery of actual conspiracy—usurper arming three ships to land at Naples, Tuscany, or France coast; sailor arrested in Marseilles secretly visited Island of Elba and carried oral message from grand-marshal to Bonapartist in Paris preparing men's minds for return. King replied praise and declared royal gratitude will never forget service. Villefort stated: "Sire, the suddenness of this event must prove to your majesty that the issue is in the hands of Providence... Do not attribute to me more than I deserve." King later mentioned General Quesnel's death, wondering if result of murder rather than suicide; met unknown person at Rue Saint-Jacques. Police minister described suspect: fifty to fifty-two years old, dark, black eyes with shaggy eyebrows, thick moustache, blue frock-coat buttoned to chin, rosette of Legion of Honor. Villefort turned red and pale, leaned on armchair; but when learned unknown had escaped, breathed again. King detached cross of Legion of Honor and gave it to Villefort. **Noirtier—Villefort's father—cut off compromising whiskers, took colored neckerchief instead of black cravat, put on Villefort's dark brown coat cut away in front, tried narrow-brimmed hat, took up bamboo switch, walked with easy swagger, passed cool and collected by two or three ill-looking men at corner of street.**

**Imprisonment, despair, and psychological dissolution (1 March afternoon/evening onward)**: Through Rue Caisserie, Rue Saint-Laurent, Rue Taramis to quay. Saw lights of La Consigne. Officer opened door; passage formed between soldier ranks. Boat drifted; four oarsmen impelled rapidly towards Pilon. Chain closing port lowered; in second they were in Frioul. Dantès saw light of Point des Catalans where Mercédès dwelt. Rose and perceived within hundred yards black and frowning Château d'If. Gendarme placed knee on chest: "Good! This is the way you keep your word as sailor!" Levelled carbine at Dantès. Dantès remained motionless, gnashing teeth, wringing hands with fury. Like man in dream; did not see ocean, terrible barrier against freedom. Followed guide into room almost underground, bare reeking walls, lamp on stool illumined apartment faintly. Jailer said: "Here is your chamber for tonight... Bread, water, and fresh straw; that is all a prisoner can wish for. Goodnight." Before Dantès could open mouth, jailer disappeared, taking lamp. Dantès alone in darkness and silence.

**Prison routine timeline (1816 onward)**: With fragment of plaster, Dantès wrote date 30th July, 1816, and made mark every day not to lose reckoning. Days and weeks passed away, then months—Dantès still waited; he at first expected to be freed in a fortnight. This fortnight expired, he decided inspector would do nothing until return to Paris, fixed three months; three months passed, then six more. Finally ten months and a half had gone by. At expiration of first year, governor transferred; new governor arrived; would-be too tedious to learn prisoners' names; learned their numbers instead. Young man was no longer called Edmond Dantès—was now number 34. Nearly four years had passed away; at end of second year he had ceased to mark lapse of time.

**Psychological torment and spiritual crisis**: Dantès passed through all stages of torture natural to prisoners in suspense. Sustained first by pride of conscious innocence; then began to doubt his own innocence; then, relaxing sentiment of pride, addressed supplications to man, not God. Wished to be amongst prisoners in order to see some other face; sighed for galleys. Asked jailer one day to let him have companion, even if mad abbé. Jailer laid request before governor; latter refused, imagining Dantès wished to conspire. Dantès had exhausted all human resources, then turned to God. All pious ideas returned; recollected prayers his mother had taught him, discovered new meaning in every word. He prayed aloud, no longer terrified at sound of his own voice. Yet in spite of earnest prayers, Dantès remained prisoner. Then gloom settled heavily. Dantès was man of great simplicity of thought, without education; could not traverse in mental vision history of ages in dungeon solitude. His energetic spirit, imprisoned like eagle in cage, clung to one idea—that of his happiness destroyed without apparent cause; he considered and reconsidered this idea, devoured it like implacable Ugolino.

**Rage, blasphemy, and decision to die**: Rage supplanted religious fervor. Dantès uttered blasphemies that made jailer recoil with horror, dashed himself furiously against walls, wreaked anger upon everything, chiefly upon himself. Letter that Villefort showed him recurred to his mind, every line gleaming forth in fiery letters on wall. He told himself that it was enmity of man, not vengeance of Heaven, that had plunged him into deepest misery. He consigned unknown persecutors to horrible tortures he could imagine, found them all insufficient because after torture came death. Before him is dead sea of azure calm, but unwary venturer finds himself struggling with monster dragging him to perdition. This state of mental anguish is less terrible than sufferings that precede it or punishment that possibly will follow. There is sort of consolation at contemplation of yawning abyss. Edmond found some solace. All sorrows and sufferings fled when angel of death seemed about to enter. Dantès reviewed past life with composure, looking forward with terror to future existence, chose middle line that seemed to afford refuge.

**Starvation resolve and execution (Year 4+ of imprisonment)**: "I wish to die," said Dantès, and had chosen manner of his death. Fearful of changing his mind, he took an oath to die. Resolved to adopt second method (refusing food, not hanging). "When my morning and evening meals are brought, I will cast them out of the window, and they will think that I have eaten them." He kept his word; twice a day he cast out through barred aperture the provisions his jailer brought—at first gayly, then with deliberation, at last with regret. Nothing but recollection of his oath gave him strength to proceed. Hunger made viands once repugnant now acceptable; he held plate in hand for an hour at a time, gazed thoughtfully at morsel of bad meat, tainted fish, black and mouldy bread. It was last yearning for life contending with resolution of despair; then his dungeon seemed less sombre, prospects less desperate. He was still young—only four or five-and-twenty—had nearly fifty years to live. What unforeseen events might not open his prison door, restore him to liberty? Then he raised to his lips repast that, like voluntary Tantalus, he refused himself; but he thought of his oath, would not break it. He persisted until had not sufficient strength to rise and cast supper out of loophole.

**Hope renewed through mysterious sound**: Next morning he could not see or hear; jailer feared he was dangerously ill. Edmond hoped he was dying. Felt sort of stupor creeping over him bringing feeling almost of content; gnawing pain at stomach had ceased; thirst had abated; when he closed eyes he saw myriads of lights dancing before them like will-o'-the-wisps that play about marshes. It was twilight of mysterious country called Death. So many loathsome animals inhabited prison that their noise did not awake him; but whether abstinence had quickened his faculties or noise was really louder, Edmond raised his head and listened. It was continual scratching, as if made by huge claw, powerful tooth, or some iron instrument attacking the stones. Although weakened, young man's brain instantly responded to idea that haunts all prisoners—liberty! It seemed to him that heaven had at length taken pity on him, had sent this noise to warn him on very brink of abyss. Perhaps one of those beloved ones he had so often thought of was thinking of him, striving to diminish distance that separated them. For week since he had resolved to die, during four days that he had been carrying out his purpose, Edmond had not spoken to attendant, had not answered him when he inquired what was matter, turned his face to wall when he looked too curiously; but now jailer might hear noise and put end to it, destroy ray of something like hope that soothed his last moments. Jailer brought him breakfast. Dantès raised himself up and began to talk about everything; about bad quality of food, coldness of dungeon, grumbling and complaining, in order to have excuse for speaking louder, wearying jailer's patience, who out of kindness of heart had brought broth and white bread. Dantès raised eyes towards soup, rose, staggered towards it, raised vessel to lips, drank off contents with feeling of indescribable pleasure. Had resolution to stop with this; had heard that shipwrecked persons had died through eagerly devouring too much food. Edmond replaced on table bread he was about to devour, returned to couch—he did not wish to die. Soon felt that his ideas became again collected—he could think, strengthen his thoughts by reasoning.

## Marius and Cosette: Courtship to Death Vigil

**Spring Year 6 confessions through barricade**: Marius revealed orphan status, lawyer profession, father colonel-hero. Cosette revealed convent upbringing, dead mother, father M. Fauchelevent. Éponine died leading Marius to barricade. Witnessed M. Mabeuf's death, Bahorel killed. Shot broke collar bone. Vigorous hand seized him before consciousness vanished.

**Medical recovery and wedding (1 February 1833)**: Doctor declared recovery assured. Learned Cosette was not daughter of old man she called father; another Fauchelevent was real father. Dowry: five hundred eighty thousand francs, constituted legacy by dead person desiring to remain unknown. **Wedding at church of Saint-Paul: Cosette wore white taffeta petticoat, Binche guipure robe, English point veil, pearl necklace, orange flower wreath. Route: Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire. Jean Valjean rose, left unperceived during celebration.**

**Javert's death and estrangement**: Javert drowned in Seine. **RUMOR—Marius suspects Jean Valjean killed Javert in barricade.**

**Jean Valjean's revelation and withdrawal**: **Proclaimed: "I am an ex-convict."** Marius shocked, concluded Jean Valjean horrible workman but admirable work. Address changed to _you_, "Madame," "Monsieur Jean." Cosette became more gay, less tender. One day chanced to say "father." "Say Jean"—She replied: "Ah! truly, Monsieur Jean." Complete extinction ensued. Neatly clad in black, emerged daily at same hour towards nightfall from Rue de l'Homme Armé. **He was eighty years old; before Marius' marriage, would have hardly been taken for fifty; that year had counted for thirty.** Later confined to apartment, then bed. **Revealed black jet from England, white jet from Norway; invented way of substituting slides; six hundred thousand francs made. Also managed very well with glass goods. Adjured Marius: "Have no fear, the six hundred thousand francs really belong to Cosette!"** **[Heard by God alone]: "All is over. I shall never see her more... What is frightful is to die without seeing her."** Final decline: breath intermittent; difficulty moving forearm; feet lost all movement. As wretchedness of limb increased, all majesty of soul displayed. Light of unknown world visible in eyes. **In cemetery of Père-Lachaise, vicinity of common grave, far from elegant quarter, in deserted corner beside old wall, beneath great yew tree over which climbs wild convolvulus, amid dandelions and mosses, lies stone.**

## Thénardier's Blackmail and Marius's Confrontation

**Thénardier's discovery and exposure**: Through daughter Azelma tracking married pair, discovered Cosette was Madame la Baronne Pontmercy. **Offered to drive individual from family who has no right there; claimed twenty thousand francs as price.** **Wore black cloth coat, silk waistcoat, boots, green glasses, plastered gray hair. With agility of monkey, tore off spectacles, withdrew two quills from nose, took off face as man takes off hat.**

**Marius's confrontation and evidence**: Revealed Javert's suicide facts announced in _Moniteur_ 15th June, 1832: Javert reported to prefect that, having been taken prisoner in barricade of Rue de la Chanvrerie, he owed his life to magnanimity of insurgent who, holding him under pistol, fired into air instead of blowing out his brains. **Marius possessed evidence, certain date, irrefragable proof. "You are an infamous wretch! you are a liar, a calumniator, a villain... you have only succeeded in glorifying him. And it is you who are the thief! And it is you who are the assassin! I saw you, Thénardier Jondrette, in that lair on the Rue de l'Hôpital."** Offered twenty thousand francs total, ordered him to America with daughter; wife dead. **The moral wretchedness of Thénardier was irremediable. He was in America what he had been in Europe. With Marius' money, Thénardier set up as slave-dealer.**
